## Communities inventing words

In this dataset, we have communities of four or eight people, inventing words for shapes that had no names (Raviv, Meyer & Lev-Ari, 2019). One quick reminder of a single turn, because its pieces become the columns of our table. One person (the producer) saw a shape and typed a made-up word for it. Their partner picked the shape they thought it meant: a hit if they were right, a miss if they were wrong. Then they swapped roles and moved on, pair after pair, for fourteen rounds.

At the start, everyone typed different nonsense. Round by round, each community drifted toward words it came to share: a small language, different in every group. Every one of those turns is in the dataset below, one row each: one word that one person produced for one shape.

The clever part is the design: **some communities were large and some were small.** That's the comparison we'll come back to. For now, just meet the data. We've put every turn into one table, where each row is **one word that one person produced for one shape**:

| column      | what it holds                                                 |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| `community` | the size of the group: `"big"` or `"small"`                   |
| `group`     | which group it was (`"g01"` … `"g24"`)                        |
| `round`     | which round of the game (1-14) — the game's clock             |
| `item`      | which shape was being described (a number, 1-28)              |
| `shape`     | the shape's family (a rough visual category)                  |
| `producer`  | which person in the group typed the word                      |
| `word`      | the made-up word they typed                                   |
| `correct`   | did the partner pick the right shape? (1 = yes, 0 = no)       |

Download it, put it in your working folder on UCloud, and load it — same two steps as the last two weeks:

``` r
# Load the tidyverse, then read the data into a table called lang.
library(tidyverse)
lang <- read_csv("language_evolution.csv")

# Look at what we've got.
glimpse(lang)
```

The column that matters most today is `round`. The whole point of the experiment is to watch what changes *over the rounds*. Words at round 1 versus round 14, so almost everything we compute will be grouped by `round`.

:::: {.predict-check data-answer="big" data-accept="big||the big ones||big groups||the big community||bigger"}
Two communities, `"big"` and `"small"`. One of them has many more rows in the table than the other. Try some code to figure out which one?

::: {.pc-explanation}
`big` has about twice as many rows. More people in a group means more producers taking turns each round, so more words get typed. That's worth remembering: the bigger community *generates more data per round* simply because it has more members.
:::
